name: Oregon
summary_text: Visitors to Oregon enter under a United States federal framework that applies in every state. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to correct what it called the misapplication of the 2020 Bostock ruling. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed these passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy that had run since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The American Civil Liberties Union is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records. Other federal measures reach the visitor directly. Screening at United States checkpoints carries an outing risk, because TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy; several foreign governments responded by issuing advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and at least eight European countries adjusted their entry guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens in March 2025. Federal custody records are adverse: from 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men have reportedly been subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. Care access is constrained: Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals in summer 2025 for full records of patients under 19, the specialised LGBTQ youth service on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline was shut down in July 2025, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court. Against that federal background, Oregon sits in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk assessment built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition. The assessment records that Oregon's laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights, and it contrasts this with the worst-law states, where penalties reach up to five years in prison or an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use. The Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Oregon as a state holding a shield law or executive order from 2023. That shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when the care provided is legal in Oregon but banned in the patient's home state, which is directly material for visitors travelling in from states with youth-care bans. The national picture behind that entry is uneven: 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38 per cent of the transgender population aged 13 and over, hold healthcare shields, while 32 states and five territories, covering 56 per cent, hold none. Youth-care bans are tracked on the same map and some have been permanently blocked in court.

name: Pennsylvania
summary_text: Travelers to Pennsylvania stand under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and issues passports only as M or F according to supporting documents; passports already carrying X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs over the changed treatment of trans passport applicants.  Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and a State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 bar visas for trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sporting events; applicants are flagged under an internal marking, and a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar. Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk through secondary screening, devices and pat-downs, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country during 2025.  Pennsylvania itself sits in the low-risk tier of Erin Reed's anti-trans national legal risk assessment as updated in July 2026, which covers states that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without specially protecting them, while documenting continued national degradation of trans rights through the 2026 legislative season.  The live legislative risk in Pennsylvania concerns school and collegiate athletics rather than adult status, documents or public facilities. The Pennsylvania Senate passed Senate Bill 1293, the Save Women's Sports Act, on 22 April 2026, which would ban transgender female athletes from girls' and women's teams in the commonwealth; Governor Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers 'extremists', and it was unclear whether the House of Representatives would take the bill up. The Senate had already approved Senate Bill 9 on 6 May 2025, reserving women's-designated teams for 'biological females' in K-12 and collegiate sports and sending it to the House.  Pennsylvania has also declined an anti-trans measure of this kind: Governor Tom Wolf vetoed comparable legislation on 11 July 2022 that would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with female-designated sports limited to athletes assigned female at birth. Both pending bills target youth sports participation rather than transgender adults or public-facility access, so a trans visitor to Pennsylvania faces no state-level restriction on restroom use, identity documents or medical care under the sources available here.
